tagline: A former toll-road approach crosses Towne Pass and drops below sea level
intro: The Death Valley Scenic Byway follows two-lane SR 190 through the national park, crossing Panamint Valley and Towne Pass before dropping into Death Valley. The Federal Highway Administration describes sculpted hills, sand dunes and a route that dips below sea level. Its archived National Scenic Byway listing gives 81.5 miles and allows two hours to drive, or four hours to enjoy the route. Towne Pass stands about 4,950 feet above sea level; Stovepipe Wells, below it to the east, stands less than ten feet above sea level.

Herman Eichbaum tried several approaches to securing a toll road before narrowing his plan to a connection between the area southeast of Darwin and his Stovepipe Wells resort. The road was certified complete in May 1926, with tolls of $2 per vehicle and 50 cents per person. The state bought it in 1934. State and National Park Service paving followed, completed in 1937 with a cutoff that bypassed Darwin and the old toll road west of Panamint Springs.

From the western park entrance, the highway curves down into Panamint Valley, then crosses Towne Pass to Stovepipe Wells. Continue southeast through the valley to Furnace Creek and the Badwater Basin turnoff. The road climbs out beside Furnace Creek Wash, then turns east at the Dante's View turnoff toward the eastern park boundary.

moments.title: Stovepipe Wells
moments.text: A length of stovepipe marked a waterhole when sand obscured it, giving Stovepipe Wells its name. The historical marker also places the waterhole at the junction of two Indigenous trails. During the mining booms at Rhyolite and Skidoo, this was the only known water source on the Cross-Valley road. A temporary settlement began in 1906 as work started on a road between those towns. Tents offered travelers food, drink and lodging. The namesake well lies northeast of the modern village. The village itself stands less than ten feet above sea level along SR 190.

moments.title: Burnt Wagons
moments.text: The monument at Burnt Wagons records a decision to abandon the vehicles that had brought gold seekers into Death Valley. Its plaque identifies the Jayhawker group of Death Valley Forty-Niners, who entered the valley in 1849 seeking a shorter route to central California's mines. They burned their wagons, dried meat from some oxen, and continued west on foot with the surviving animals. The former settlement near Stovepipe Wells is registered as California Historical Landmark 441.

moments.title: Furnace Creek
moments.text: Springs in the Amargosa Range created the natural oasis here. Green alfalfa fields gave Greenland Ranch its first name in 1883. A weather station followed in 1891, and the ranch became Furnace Creek Ranch in 1933. The weather station recorded 134°F on July 10, 1913, a measurement whose accuracy some meteorologists dispute. The village stands 190 feet below sea level and houses the national park visitor center, museum and headquarters. At the visitor center on SR 190, exhibits and a film cover the geology, climate, wildlife and human history of the park.
